# Book III, Proposition 23

*Similar segments on the same straight line cannot be unequal*

> On the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/23-idea.svg" alt="Two different segments of circles on the same straight line (blue) and on the same side never hold equal angles: the angle in the inner one (red) is always the greater. So similar segments there are one and the same." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Two different segments of circles on the same straight line (blue) and on the same side never hold equal angles: the angle in the inner one (red) is always the greater. So similar segments there are one and the same.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/23.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.23, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For, if possible, on the same straight line AB let two similar and unequal segments of circles ACB, ADB be constructed on the same side;

let ACD be drawn through, and let CB, DB be joined.

Then, since the segment ACB is similar to the segment ADB,

and similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, [III. Def. 11]

the angle ACB is equal to the angle ADB, the exterior to the interior: which is impossible. [I. 16]

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookIII/Prop23.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Prop23.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- On the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of
circles on the same side. -/
theorem Prop23 {A B C D : Point} {ACB ADB : Circle} (hACB : ∃ O : Point, Centre O ACB)
    (hADB : ∃ O : Point, Centre O ADB) (hA₁ : OnCircle A ACB) (hB₁ : OnCircle B ACB)
    (hC : OnCircle C ACB) (hA₂ : OnCircle A ADB) (hB₂ : OnCircle B ADB)
    (hD : OnCircle D ADB) (hCD : SameSideOf C D A B) (hsim : ∠ A C B = ∠ A D B) :
    ACB = ADB := by
  -- For, if possible, on the same straight line AB let two similar and unequal segments of
  -- circles ACB, ADB be constructed on the same side;
  refine Classical.byContradiction fun hne => ?_
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hCD.triangle
  have hAB : A ≠ B := hCD.1
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := hABC.off_line hA_AB hB_AB
  -- let ACD be drawn through, and let CB, DB be joined.
  /- Euclid draws the segment ACB within ADB. The circles meet at `A` and `B`, so not at
     `C` as well [III. 10]: `C` is within the circle ADB, or outside it. Within, `AC`
     drawn through meets ADB at `D₀` beyond `C` (System E, Intersections 5), and the angle
     `ADB` is the angle `AD₀B`, in the same segment [III. 21]. Outside, the segments are
     the other way about: a point `M` between `A` and `B` is within both circles, so `MC`
     meets ADB at a point `D₁` within ACB (Intersections 4, Circle 2), and `AD₁` drawn
     through meets ACB at `C₀`. Either way a point `P` of one segment lies within the other,
     and `AP` drawn through meets it at `Q`. -/
  have hC₂ : ¬ OnCircle C ADB := fun hC₂ =>
    hne (Prop10 hACB hADB hA₁ hA₂ hB₁ hB₂ hC hC₂ hAB hABC.ne₁₃ hABC.ne₂₃)
  obtain ⟨P, Q, hAPQ, hP_AB, hangles⟩ : ∃ P Q : Point, Between A P Q ∧ ¬ OnLine P AB ∧
      ((∠ A P B = ∠ A C B ∧ ∠ A Q B = ∠ A D B) ∨
        (∠ A P B = ∠ A D B ∧ ∠ A Q B = ∠ A C B)) := by
    by_cases hin : InsideCircle C ADB
    · obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hABC.ne₁₃
      obtain ⟨D₀, hD₀, -, hD₀CA⟩ := line_circle_beyond hin hC_AC hA_AC hABC.ne₁₃
      have hD₀C : SameSideOf D₀ C A B :=
        SameSideOf.of_onRay (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hD₀CA))
          (SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB (same_side_refl hC_AB))
      exact ⟨C, D₀, between_symm hD₀CA, hC_AB,
        Or.inl ⟨rfl, (Prop21 hADB hD hA₂ hB₂ hD₀ (hCD.symm.trans hD₀C.symm)).symm⟩⟩
    · obtain ⟨M, hM_AB, hAMB, -⟩ := exists_point_between hA_AB hB_AB hAB []
      have hM₁ : InsideCircle M ACB := inside_of_between (Or.inr hA₁) (Or.inr hB₁) hAMB
      have hM₂ : InsideCircle M ADB := inside_of_between (Or.inr hA₂) (Or.inr hB₂) hAMB
      have hMC : M ≠ C := fun h => hC_AB (h ▸ hM_AB)
      obtain ⟨MC, hM_MC, hC_MC⟩ := Postulate1 M C hMC
      obtain ⟨D₁, hD₁, hD₁_MC, hMD₁C⟩ := line_circle_between hM₂ hM_MC ⟨hin, hC₂⟩ hC_MC
      have hD₁_in : InsideCircle D₁ ACB := inside_of_between (Or.inl hM₁) (Or.inr hC) hMD₁C
      have hD₁_AB : ¬ OnLine D₁ AB := fun h =>
        hC_AB (line_unique (ne_of_between hMD₁C) hM_MC hD₁_MC hM_AB h ▸ hC_MC)
      have hD₁C : SameSideOf D₁ C A B :=
        SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB (pasch2 hMD₁C hM_AB hD₁_AB)
      have hAD₁ : A ≠ D₁ := fun h => hD₁_AB (h ▸ hA_AB)
      obtain ⟨AD₁, hA_AD₁, hD₁_AD₁⟩ := Postulate1 A D₁ hAD₁
      obtain ⟨C₀, hC₀, -, hC₀D₁A⟩ := line_circle_beyond hD₁_in hD₁_AD₁ hA_AD₁ hAD₁
      have hC₀D₁ : SameSideOf C₀ D₁ A B :=
        SameSideOf.of_onRay (OnRay.of_beyond (between_symm hC₀D₁A))
          (SameSideOf.of_line hAB hA_AB hB_AB (same_side_refl hD₁_AB))
      exact ⟨D₁, C₀, between_symm hC₀D₁A, hD₁_AB, Or.inr
        ⟨(Prop21 hADB hD hA₂ hB₂ hD₁ (hCD.symm.trans hD₁C.symm)).symm,
         (Prop21 hACB hC hA₁ hB₁ hC₀ (hD₁C.symm.trans hC₀D₁.symm)).symm⟩⟩
  -- Then, since the segment ACB is similar to the segment ADB,
  -- and similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, [III. Def. 11]
  have hPQ : ∠ A P B = ∠ A Q B := by
    rcases hangles with ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ | ⟨h₁, h₂⟩
    · rw [h₁, h₂]; exact hsim
    · rw [h₁, h₂]; exact hsim.symm
  -- the angle ACB is equal to the angle ADB, the exterior to the interior: which is
  -- impossible. [I. 16]
  obtain ⟨AP, hA_AP, hP_AP⟩ := Postulate1 A P (ne_of_between hAPQ)
  have hQ_AP : OnLine Q AP := on_line_of_between hAPQ hA_AP hP_AP
  have hB_AP : ¬ OnLine B AP := fun h =>
    hP_AB (line_unique hAB hA_AP h hA_AB hB_AB ▸ hP_AP)
  have hQPB : Triangle Q P B :=
    Triangle.of_line hQ_AP hP_AP (ne_of_between (between_symm hAPQ)) hB_AP
  have h16 := (BookI.Prop16 hQPB.cab (between_symm hAPQ)).1
  rw [angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hAPQ)) hQPB.ne₁₃.symm,
    angle_symm hQPB.ne₂₃.symm (ne_of_between hAPQ), ← hPQ] at h16
  exact lt_irrefl _ h16
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**The exterior cannot equal the interior.** Euclid draws AC through to D and joins CB, DB. The angle ACB is exterior to the triangle DCB, and ADB is interior and opposite to it; similar segments would make them equal, and I.16 makes the exterior greater. Euclid's "cannot be constructed" is the phrase of I.7, Heath observes (vol. 2, p. 53), and both impossibilities become equalities in our statements: in I.7 the two points are one, and here the two circles are one.

**Similar before similarity.** Heath reports Augustus De Morgan's objection to Definition III.11: "De Morgan remarks that the use of the word *similar* in 'similar segments' is an anticipation, and that similarity *of form* is meant. He adds that the definition is a theorem, or would be if 'similar' had taken its final meaning" (vol. 2, p. 5). Similar figures wait for Book VI. We take the definition as Euclid gives it, equal angles at one point of each segment, and III.21 makes the angle the same at every point of each.

**Which segment lies within?** Euclid draws ACB inside ADB without a word. Robert Simson observes, and Heath agrees, that the remark Euclid makes in III.24, that the circles cannot meet again, "is an equally necessary preliminary to III. 23, in order that we may be justified in drawing the segments as being one inside the other" (vol. 2, p. 53). Lean begins as Simson does: the circles meet at A and B, so not at C (III.10), and C is within ADB or outside it. Our D may lie anywhere on its segment, and III.21 carries its angle to where AC drawn through meets ADB, or, with the segments the other way about, carries both angles. Then I.16 does Euclid's work.

**"Not coinciding with one another."** Simson puts these words for Euclid's "unequal" (Heath, vol. 2, p. 53), and they are just what our equality of circles says. Christopher Clavius and the other early editors add that similar segments on opposite sides of one straight line are equal too: turn one about the base until it lies on the other's side. We state the case Euclid proves, for on opposite sides the segments may lie in different circles.

**The modern way.** For a straight line AB of length c > 0 and 0 < θ < π, the points on one side of AB that see it under the angle θ fill a single open arc of one circle, whose centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB at signed distance (c/2) cot θ toward that side. The angle and the side fix the circle.
